references.text: God's original command to Adam not to eat from the tree of knowledge, with a warning of death. In 3:3, Eve adds that they must not even touch the tree, which is not part of the original command.
Eva broke God's command and ate fruit from the forbidden tree, and also gave some to Adam. This is the direct consequence of failing to follow the command mentioned in verse 3.
Paul explains how sin entered the world through one man (Adam), and death through sin—a direct result of breaking God's command in the Garden of Eden.
Paul warns that just as the serpent deceived Eve with his cunning, so too may the thoughts of believers be led astray from sincere devotion to Christ.
Paul notes that it was Eve who was deceived and fell into transgression, referring directly to the events in Genesis 3.
The original command (2:17) and humanity's restatement of it before the fall (3:3) form a coherent theological unity regarding the terms of the covenant.
The warning of death for eating from the tree of knowledge (3:3) stands in direct contrast to being barred from the tree of life (3:22) as a result of breaking that warning.
The general permission to eat from all trees (2:16) sets the framework for the specific command (3:3), which defines human freedom and responsibility.
